chapter: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
title: Success in the Follies and cutting the act to nine minutes
summary: They stood out in vagabond clothes and Bubbles' down-to-earth style; he cut the act to nine minutes in rehearsal and still stopped the show when the stage manager threatened to cut the lights.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: We go in this show, man, and never look back. Never look back. It was the greatest show that we ever had in life. Greatest showtime, because we did the shows and the shows were so pleasing that we stood out like a sore thumb, you know. We were the only ones that had vagabond clothes on in the show. We were the only ones that had dancing of the style that we were doing it, 'cause Mitzi Mayfair was a dancer and so was Harry Leroy, but they were a different style. I had the down-to-earth style, you see and they could borrow with me more than they could with any one of them and that's what set us apart, man. When nobody wanted to follow

our act, they'd change our act. They'd change the position of our act on every show until finally they got us down to where we could only go on next to closing and after us came the finale. Harry Richman singing the finale. "Get the beat, of people's feet, walking up and down the street, Going to New York" That was the finale of the show and after we did our number, did our song and all, next comes on the finale. In other words, while we were doing -- we rehearsed about five hours over at Nazarro's hotel to get this act down where the manager of the theater wants the act down from 14 to 9. We don't know what five minutes to cut out of the act, 'cause it's so interwoven, you know. So we're working, we're working, we're working. Every time Buck would say, it's 5 o'clock, it's time to go home from the rehearsal. No, we can't go nowhere from rehearsal, got to get the act down first. And he made me so angry trying to get over there to do the rehearsal.

He made me so mad that I couldn't say nothing to him, but shut up, man, you don't know what you're talking about. Let's get this time down. So I worked on this time and I got it down to where I know it was no more than 9 minutes, you know? And we go over there. And that's all they wanted to know, did we have the act down to 9 minutes. Okay, that's good. Didn't have to do no kind of show at all. When it come time to go on the stage, we went on the stage. Now we got the act in rehearsal to 9 minutes, man. And I know how to maneuver the act to keep it in that category. And would you believe, that I got the first song done, I'm in the second number, Buck's going to play the solo and I'm going down to the dance when I go in the dance from one side of the stage, from the right to the left, the stage manager says, "You're over time, I'm going to put the lights out." That did it. Now, I'm going to dance back and tell Buck about it and something says, no, don't tell him -- same as the

other thing I told you about, they didn't want negroes in the theater -- I was going to tell him then but I didn't tell him. I didn't tell him about what the stage manager said, they're going to put the lights out. I just danced over there to him and then danced back to the center of the stage and finished the act out as I would finish without him knowing a thing and come on off the stage. And it was a sensation and there was no overtime.
